summary: Defines the standard format for interchanging network news messages between USENET hosts, reflecting version B2.11 of the News program. It updates and replaces RFC 850. The RFC says it does not specify an Internet standard, and it was replaced by RFC 5536 and RFC 5537.

eli5.summary: It is the rule for how a posted message must be written so any news computer can read it and pass it along to others.

questions: what is the usenet message format
what headers are required in usenet messages
how are messages batched in usenet
subtitle: Standard header and transmission format for network news messages across USENET hosts.

tldr.problem: USENET needed a consistent message format so news messages could be reliably exchanged between different host systems and news readers.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1036 specifies that all USENET news messages must be formatted as valid Internet mail messages (RFC 822), with required headers like From, Date, Newsgroups, Subject, Message-ID, and Path, plus optional headers for control messages, distribution, and other metadata.
tldr.outcome: This standard enabled USENET to operate as a unified logical network across diverse physical networks (UUCP, Internet, Ethernet, etc.). It was replaced by RFC 5536 and RFC 5537, which modernized the format.

today: RFC 1036 is obsolete. It was replaced by RFC 5536 and RFC 5537, which modernize the USENET message standard for contemporary use. USENET itself has largely faded from mainstream use, though it remains active in limited communities.

sections.title: Introduction and Design Principles
sections.content:
RFC 1036 defines the standard format for interchanging network news messages among USENET hosts. It updates and replaces RFC 850, reflecting the B2.11 version of the News program. The standard is designed to be compatible with existing tools for both mail and news by adopting the Internet mail format (RFC 822) as the foundation, with additional restrictions and requirements specific to USENET.

USENET is a logical network built on top of multiple physical networks including UUCP (Unix-to-Unix Copy), the Internet, Ethernet, BLICN, NSC Hyperchannel, and BERKNET. The standard ensures that news messages can travel across all these different physical networks while maintaining consistent format and semantics.
sections.eli5: USENET is a way for computers to share messages like a big bulletin board. Different computers might be connected by different cables and methods, but they all need to agree on how messages should be written so everyone can read them correctly.

sections.title: Required and Optional Headers
sections.content:
A standard USENET message consists of header lines followed by a blank line and then the message body. Required header lines include From (sender's email address and optional full name), Date (when posted, in RFC 822 format), Newsgroups (comma-separated list of groups), Subject (message topic), Message-ID (unique identifier in angle brackets), and Path (the route taken through hosts).

Optional header lines include Followup-To (where replies should go), Expires (suggested expiration date), Reply-To (reply destination), Sender (who submitted if different from From), References (Message-IDs of related messages), Control (control message commands), Distribution (distribution scope), Keywords, Summary, Approved (for moderated groups), Lines (count of body lines), Xref (local cross-reference to message numbers), and Organization (sender's organization).
sections.eli5: Every USENET message needs basic information like who sent it, when it was sent, and what newsgroup it belongs to. Some messages can have extra headers for special purposes, like saying when the message should be deleted or who approved it.

sections.title: Control Messages and Network Administration
sections.content:
Control messages are special messages used for communication among USENET host machines rather than user reading. They are distributed through the same newsgroup mechanism as ordinary messages but contain commands in the Control header or Subject line.

Standard control message types include: cancel (delete a previous message), ihave/sendme (negotiate article transfer to reduce redundant traffic), newgroup (create a new newsgroup, requires Approved header), rmgroup (remove a newsgroup, requires Approved header), sendsys (request the sys file listing neighbors), version (request software version), and checkgroups (verify active newsgroup list). These mechanisms enable USENET administrators to manage the network's topology and content distribution without manual intervention on every host.
sections.eli5: Computers on USENET send special control messages to each other to manage the network itself: creating new discussion groups, removing old ones, or asking "do you have this message so I don't send it again?" These are like behind-the-scenes instructions, not messages people read.

sections.title: Transmission Methods and Batching
sections.content:
USENET messages can be transmitted between neighboring hosts through several methods. Remote execution spools the rnews command with the message on standard input over UUCP or Berknet. Transfer by mail sends messages as email (either directly or encapsulated with N prefixes to protect headers) to user newsmail or rnews on the remote system.

Batching combines multiple messages into one transmission to reduce overhead. Batched messages are prefixed with #! rnews <length> headers indicating the byte count of each message. The unbatcher on the receiving system parses these headers and extracts individual messages. This optimization is important because news messages are typically short, and the overhead of UUCP spooling sometimes exceeds the cost of sending individual messages.
sections.eli5: To send USENET messages between computers, you can run a command directly, send email, or batch multiple messages together to save time. Batching works by putting a length marker before each message so the receiving computer knows where one message ends and another begins.

sections.title: News Propagation Algorithm
sections.content:
USENET is modeled as a directed graph where nodes are host computers and arcs are transmission paths. Messages propagate through this network according to a standardized algorithm: each host maintains a sys file listing its neighbors and which newsgroups to send to each. When a host receives a message, it adds its own name to the Path header (showing the route traveled) and forwards the message to neighbors that subscribe to the relevant newsgroups.

The Path header prevents redundant traffic by showing which hosts have already received a message. When a message arrives with a host's name in the Path, that host will not send it back to the originating host. This routing mechanism allows USENET to propagate news efficiently across multiple independent systems while preventing message loops and duplicate delivery. The sys file format is standardized so network administrators can reliably exchange topology information via the sendsys control message.
sections.eli5: USENET is like a chain of telephone operators passing a message along. Each computer adds its name to the path, so when the message gets to the next computer, that one won't send it back to where it came from. That keeps messages moving forward and prevents the same message from going in circles forever.
